title: Diseases of Increased Intracranial Fluid: Cerebral Edema and Hydrocephalus
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: The adult skull is a rigid container, so any extra water in brain tissue (cerebral edema) or extra cerebrospinal fluid (hydrocephalus) must displace something else before pressure rises. This chapter explains the three main types of cerebral edema, how rising intracranial pressure produces papilledema, the Cushing triad, and herniation, and how blocked flow or failed absorption of CSF enlarges the ventricles. It then contrasts normal pressure hydrocephalus and idiopathic intracranial hypertension, two disorders that look paradoxical until the pressure physics is clear. Board questions usually give a scan, a pupil, a gait, or an opening pressure and ask you to name the mechanism or the site of obstruction.
prerequisites: CSF production, circulation, and absorption, and the ventricular system (NE-4, NE-10)
Structure of the blood-brain barrier: endothelial tight junctions, basement membrane, astrocyte end-feet
Na+/K+ ATPase and osmotic water movement across cell membranes
Dural folds (falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli) and the foramen magnum (NE-3, NE-4)
Course and functions of CN II, III, and VI (NE-8)

connections.how: Large infarcts and intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage cause edema, raised pressure, and later communicating hydrocephalus.
Tumors cause vasogenic edema and, when they sit in or near the ventricles, obstructive hydrocephalus.
Abscesses produce vasogenic edema, and meningitis scars the arachnoid granulations and causes communicating hydrocephalus.
Aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II malformation with myelomeningocele, and Dandy-Walker malformation are developmental causes of noncommunicating hydrocephalus.
Cerebral perfusion pressure depends on mean arterial pressure, and the Cushing reflex uses sympathetic outflow and the baroreceptor reflex.

terms.def: The pressure inside the skull, normally about 5 to 15 mmHg in a resting supine adult.
Because the skull volume is fixed, an increase in brain, blood, CSF, or a mass must be offset by a decrease in one of the others.
The pressure driving blood through the brain, equal to mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure.
Extracellular brain edema caused by breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, mainly in white matter.
Intracellular swelling of neurons and glia when energy failure stops the Na+/K+ ATPase, with the barrier initially intact.
Movement of CSF across the ependyma into periventricular white matter when ventricular pressure is high, as in obstructive hydrocephalus.
Swelling of the optic discs caused by raised intracranial pressure, usually bilateral.
Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing caused by brainstem compression and ischemia, a late sign of raised ICP.
Displacement of brain tissue across a dural fold or through the foramen magnum by a pressure gradient between compartments.
Ventricular enlargement in which CSF passes freely from the ventricles to the subarachnoid space but is not absorbed normally.
Enlargement of the ventricles that simply fills the space left by lost brain tissue, with normal pressure.
A deficit, such as a CN VI palsy, caused by raised pressure or brain shift rather than by a lesion at the site the deficit suggests.

sections.title: Cerebral edema, raised intracranial pressure, and its complications

blocks.text: The adult cranial vault holds roughly 80% brain, 10% blood, and 10% CSF. By the Monro-Kellie doctrine, added volume is first buffered by shifting CSF into the spinal canal and blood out of the venous sinuses. Once that reserve is used up, each further milliliter raises ICP steeply, so patients can deteriorate abruptly after a stable period.
Three edema types, defined by where water sits

In vasogenic edema the tight junctions of brain capillaries open and protein-rich plasma leaks into the extracellular space. The fluid spreads along loosely packed white matter tracts while dense cortex is relatively spared. This is the edema around tumors (whose new vessels lack a normal barrier), abscesses, and contusions, and it is why glucocorticoids, which reduce tumor capillary permeability, shrink peritumoral edema but not ischemic edema.

In cytotoxic edema the barrier is initially intact. Ischemia or hypoxia depletes ATP, the Na+/K+ ATPase stops, Na+ accumulates inside neurons and astrocytes, and water follows. Both gray and white matter swell within minutes, and because water is trapped inside cells, diffusion-weighted MRI shows restricted diffusion, the earliest imaging sign of infarction. Within days the injured barrier leaks, so a large infarct becomes mixed edema that usually peaks around days 3 to 5. Interstitial edema arises when high ventricular pressure in obstructive hydrocephalus drives CSF across the ependyma into periventricular white matter.

blocks.title: Types of cerebral edema
blocks.caption: Osmotic edema (acute hyponatremia) is sometimes listed as a fourth type.

blocks.text: Complications explained by mechanism

Papilledema develops because the subarachnoid space extends along the optic nerve sheath. Raised CSF pressure compresses axons at the lamina cribrosa and blocks axoplasmic flow, so the axons and disc swell over hours to days, enlarging the blind spot while sparing acuity until late. Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure (MAP) minus ICP, so rising ICP threatens brainstem perfusion, and the Cushing reflex raises MAP to restore it.

blocks.title: Rising ICP to the Cushing triad
steps: CSF and venous buffering exhausted
ICP rises, cerebral perfusion pressure falls
Brainstem ischemia drives sympathetic discharge: hypertension
Baroreceptors respond: vagal bradycardia
Medullary compression: irregular respiration
blocks.caption: The hypertension is compensatory; the bradycardia is a baroreflex.

blocks.title: Worked example: perfusion pressure as ICP rises
blocks.text: With MAP 90 mmHg and ICP 15 mmHg, CPP is 75 mmHg. A hematoma raises ICP to 45 mmHg; with MAP unchanged, CPP falls to 45 mmHg, below the autoregulatory range, and the brainstem becomes ischemic. Sympathetic discharge raises MAP to 130 mmHg, restoring CPP to 85 mmHg, and the baroreflex slows the heart. The hypertension protects perfusion rather than causing harm.

Herniation occurs when pressure differs across the falx, tentorium, or foramen magnum, and each syndrome follows from neighboring structures. Pupillary fibers lie on the outer surface of CN III, so in uncal herniation an ipsilateral dilated pupil precedes ptosis and a down-and-out eye.

blocks.title: Herniation syndromes
rows: Ipsilateral CN III, PCA, cerebral peduncle
Ipsilateral dilated pupil, contralateral hemianopia, contralateral hemiparesis
Hemiparesis on side of mass (false localizing)
blocks.caption: Lumbar puncture with a mass present can drive tonsillar herniation.

blocks.predict: A left temporal mass causes a dilated left pupil and right weakness. What does a new right homonymous hemianopia mean?
blocks.explain: The uncus can compress the left posterior cerebral artery, infarcting the left occipital lobe, which serves the right visual field.
blocks.check: The uncal row of the herniation table.

sections.title: Noncommunicating, communicating, and ex vacuo hydrocephalus

blocks.text: Hydrocephalus is an excess of CSF within the ventricles caused by obstructed flow or failed absorption. An adult has about 150 mL of CSF and makes about 500 mL a day, mostly from the choroid plexus, so the whole volume turns over about three times daily. Production is largely independent of pressure, so any block causes fluid to accumulate upstream within hours to days.

blocks.title: CSF circulation
steps: Choroid plexus secretes CSF into the lateral ventricles
Interventricular foramina (of Monro) to the third ventricle
Cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle
Median and lateral apertures (Magendie, Luschka) to the subarachnoid space
Arachnoid granulations drain CSF into the dural venous sinuses
blocks.caption: A block anywhere from the foramina of Monro to the fourth ventricle apertures causes noncommunicating hydrocephalus; failure at the granulations causes communicating hydrocephalus.

blocks.text: In noncommunicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus, CSF cannot leave the ventricular system, so only the ventricles upstream of the block enlarge. Aqueductal stenosis is a classic cause of congenital hydrocephalus; it may be inherited in an X-linked form (L1CAM mutation) or follow gliosis after intrauterine infection or hemorrhage. In Chiari II malformation a small posterior fossa forces the cerebellar vermis and the medulla down through the foramen magnum, almost always with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele, and outflow from the fourth ventricle is obstructed. Dandy-Walker malformation combines a hypoplastic or absent vermis with cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle and an enlarged posterior fossa. Tumors obstruct at predictable sites: a colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro, a pineal tumor compressing the aqueduct, and posterior fossa tumors of childhood compressing the fourth ventricle.

In communicating hydrocephalus, CSF passes freely into the subarachnoid space but is not absorbed. Blood after subarachnoid hemorrhage, or inflammatory exudate after meningitis, scars the arachnoid granulations and the basal subarachnoid space, so all four ventricles enlarge. Raised venous sinus pressure reduces absorption by the same logic, because CSF drains only while its pressure exceeds sinus pressure.

Hydrocephalus ex vacuo is not a CSF disorder. When neurons are lost, as in Alzheimer disease, frontotemporal dementia, or Huntington disease (where caudate atrophy enlarges the frontal horns), the ventricles and sulci enlarge together to fill the space, and pressure is normal. True hydrocephalus shows ventricles out of proportion to the sulci, often with periventricular interstitial edema.

blocks.title: Worked example: locating the obstruction on imaging
blocks.text: Enlarged lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle place the block in the cerebral aqueduct. Enlargement of only the lateral ventricles, sometimes on one side, points to the foramina of Monro, as with a colloid cyst. Enlargement of all four ventricles means either an outlet block of the fourth ventricle, as in Dandy-Walker malformation, or failed absorption at the granulations. The history separates them: a posterior fossa cyst suggests outlet block, while prior meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage suggests communicating hydrocephalus. Enlarged ventricles with equally widened sulci and no periventricular edema suggest ex vacuo change.

Head enlargement occurs only in infants because the cranial sutures are unfused and the anterior fontanelle stays open until about 12 to 18 months. The skull expands under pressure, so head circumference crosses percentiles, the fontanelle bulges, sutures separate, and scalp veins distend. A dilated third ventricle presses on the dorsal midbrain and impairs upgaze, producing the setting-sun sign. Because the skull can expand, papilledema is less common in infants than in older children and adults, who instead present with headache, vomiting, papilledema, and CN VI palsy.

blocks.predict: An infant with an enlarging head has dilated lateral and third ventricles and a small fourth ventricle. Where is the block, and why is the fourth ventricle spared?
blocks.explain: The cerebral aqueduct; CSF made upstream cannot reach the fourth ventricle, which receives only its own small choroid plexus output and drains normally.
blocks.check: Compare with the CSF circulation flow and the worked example.

blocks.text: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is a chronic communicating hydrocephalus of older adults, usually after age 60, in which the ventricles enlarge while lumbar opening pressure is normal or only mildly raised. Most cases are idiopathic; secondary NPH can follow subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, or head trauma, which scar the absorptive pathways. The name is somewhat misleading, because continuous monitoring often shows intermittent pressure waves, especially during sleep, superimposed on a normal baseline.

The leading explanation is that CSF absorption is impaired and the brain becomes less compliant, so each arterial pulse transmits a larger pressure swing into the ventricles. By the law of Laplace, wall tension rises with radius as well as pressure, so once the ventricles have enlarged, a near-normal pressure can keep stretching them. This explanation, first proposed by Hakim, is widely taught but not proven.
Why the triad appears

The enlarged lateral ventricles stretch and compress the surrounding white matter, and the clinical triad follows from which fibers lie closest. Gait disturbance is usually first and most prominent. Corticospinal and frontal-subcortical fibers serving the legs pass close to the ventricular walls, so walking becomes slow, broad-based, and short-stepped, with the feet barely clearing the floor, as though held by a magnet. Starting and turning are especially hard, while arm swing and upper limb function are relatively preserved, and there is no rest tremor.

Urinary urgency and then incontinence follow because frontal pathways that normally inhibit the spinal and pontine micturition reflexes are disrupted, producing an uninhibited bladder. The dementia is subcortical in pattern: slowed thinking, apathy, and poor attention and executive function, with less memory loss and none of the aphasia or apraxia typical of Alzheimer disease. Imaging shows ventricles enlarged out of proportion to the cortical sulci; an Evans index (frontal horn width divided by maximal inner skull width) above 0.3 indicates ventriculomegaly, and many patients have tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures.

blocks.title: From impaired absorption to the NPH triad
steps: CSF absorption at granulations is impaired
Ventricles enlarge slowly; baseline pressure stays near normal
Enlarged ventricles stretch periventricular white matter
Leg-related fibers disrupted: magnetic gait
Frontal bladder inhibition lost: urgency, incontinence
Frontal-subcortical circuits disrupted: slowed cognition, apathy
blocks.caption: Gait usually appears first and responds best to CSF removal; cognition responds least.

blocks.text: Removing 30 to 50 mL of CSF by lumbar puncture (the tap test) reduces the stretch, and a measurable improvement in gait within hours to a day supports the diagnosis. A negative test does not exclude NPH, because the test is specific but not very sensitive.

blocks.title: NPH compared with its common mimics
rows: Ventricles out of proportion to sulci
blocks.caption: The comparison rests on which structures are affected: periventricular fibers, cortex, or the nigrostriatal pathway.

blocks.text: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), also called pseudotumor cerebri, is raised ICP with no mass, no hydrocephalus, no venous sinus thrombosis, and normal CSF composition. About 90% of patients are women, typically of childbearing age with obesity or recent weight gain. It is the mirror image of NPH: pressure is clearly high, yet the ventricles are normal or small. A common explanation is that the pressure is raised evenly throughout the subarachnoid space and ventricles, so there is no pressure gradient across the brain to push the ventricles outward.
Proposed mechanisms

The cause is not fully known, and several mechanisms likely combine. CSF absorption into the dural sinuses depends on CSF pressure exceeding venous sinus pressure. Most patients have narrowing of the transverse sinuses, and raised ICP itself can compress these thin-walled sinuses, raising venous pressure and further reducing absorption. Obesity may contribute by raising intra-abdominal, intrathoracic, and therefore cerebral venous pressure, and adipose tissue is hormonally active. Excess vitamin A and retinoid drugs, tetracycline-class antibiotics, growth hormone, and withdrawal of corticosteroids are recognized associations; when such a trigger is present, many authors call the condition secondary intracranial hypertension.

blocks.title: Proposed venous feedback loop in IIH
steps: ICP rises
Thin-walled transverse sinuses are compressed
Venous sinus pressure rises
CSF absorption at granulations falls
CSF volume and ICP rise further
blocks.caption: A proposed self-sustaining loop; it explains why sinus narrowing can be both a cause and a consequence of raised pressure.

blocks.text: Findings explained by mechanism

Headache is daily and often worse when lying down. Papilledema is bilateral and causes transient visual obscurations, blackouts of vision lasting seconds with standing or bending, as swollen axons briefly lose perfusion. Field loss begins as an enlarged blind spot and peripheral, often inferonasal, constriction, while central acuity is preserved until late. Pulsatile tinnitus reflects turbulent flow through narrowed transverse sinuses. Horizontal diplopia comes from CN VI palsy, a false localizing sign: the abducens nerve has a long course up the clivus and bends over the petrous apex, so raised pressure stretches it without a focal lesion along the nerve.

blocks.title: Diagnostic findings in IIH and their meaning
rows: Raised pressure without a space-occupying cause
Partially empty sella, flattened posterior globes, distended optic nerve sheaths
Venous outflow contribution; thrombosis would make it secondary
At or above 25 cm H2O in adults (normal about 10 to 20)
blocks.caption: Opening pressure is measured with the patient lying on one side; 1 mmHg equals about 1.36 cm H2O.

blocks.text: The major complication is permanent vision loss. Sustained papilledema leads to ischemia and death of optic nerve axons, and the swollen disc gives way to a pale, atrophic one. A disc that looks less swollen over time can therefore signal axon loss rather than recovery, which is why visual fields, not disc appearance alone, track the risk.

blocks.predict: An obese 28-year-old woman taking minocycline for acne has headache, horizontal diplopia, and bilateral disc swelling. Imaging is normal. Predict the opening pressure and CSF content, and explain the diplopia.
blocks.explain: Opening pressure is raised and CSF content normal; raised pressure stretches CN VI along its long course over the petrous apex, weakening abduction.
blocks.check: Compare with the findings paragraph and the IIH table.

integration.text: Every disorder in this chapter is a problem of volume in a fixed box, so anatomy predicts the signs. The dural folds and foramen magnum define the herniation routes, the optic nerve sheath carries CSF pressure to the disc, and the long course of CN VI makes it vulnerable to any rise in pressure. Physiology supplies the numbers: CPP equals MAP minus ICP, and CSF drains only while its pressure exceeds venous sinus pressure, which links IIH and communicating hydrocephalus to venous outflow.

The most useful distinction is between pressure and ventricle size, which do not always move together. Obstructive and communicating hydrocephalus raise both; IIH raises pressure with normal ventricles; NPH enlarges ventricles with near-normal pressure; ex vacuo change enlarges ventricles only because brain is lost. Edema type is decided by where water sits, which is why diffusion MRI separates early ischemia from tumor edema. These are teaching categories, and real lesions such as large infarcts and contusions often combine more than one.

summary: The skull is a fixed volume, so added brain water, blood, CSF, or mass raises ICP steeply once CSF and venous buffering is exhausted.

Vasogenic edema is extracellular, from barrier breakdown around tumors, abscesses, and contusions; cytotoxic edema is intracellular, from Na+/K+ ATPase failure in ischemia; interstitial edema is CSF forced across the ependyma in obstructive hydrocephalus.
CPP equals MAP minus ICP; the Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) is a late compensatory sign of brainstem ischemia.
Uncal herniation compresses ipsilateral CN III (pupil first), the posterior cerebral artery, and the cerebral peduncle; tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla.

Noncommunicating hydrocephalus enlarges only ventricles upstream of a block (aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II, Dandy-Walker, tumor); communicating hydrocephalus enlarges all ventricles after granulation scarring from meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Hydrocephalus ex vacuo is ventricular enlargement from brain loss with normal pressure and proportionally widened sulci.
Infants with open sutures develop an enlarging head, bulging fontanelle, and setting-sun eyes rather than early papilledema.
NPH in older adults causes magnetic gait, urinary incontinence, and subcortical dementia from periventricular stretch, with gait improving after CSF removal.

IIH in obese women of childbearing age causes headache, papilledema, transient visual obscurations, and CN VI palsy, with normal imaging, normal CSF content, and opening pressure of 25 cm H2O or more.
Vitamin A excess, retinoids, and tetracyclines are classic associations of IIH, and permanent vision loss from optic atrophy is its main complication.

verify: Normal adult ICP (about 5 to 15 mmHg) and the threshold for intracranial hypertension (usually above 20 to 22 mmHg) vary slightly between references.

The IIH opening pressure criterion of 25 cm H2O or more in adults (28 cm H2O in children) follows the revised diagnostic criteria of Friedman and colleagues (2013); the upper limit of normal opening pressure is quoted from 20 to 25 cm H2O, higher in obese adults. Confirm the values NABNE expects.
Whether drug-associated cases (vitamin A, retinoids, tetracyclines) are called idiopathic or secondary intracranial hypertension differs between sources; the competency groups them under IIH.
Opening pressure in NPH is described as normal or mildly raised; the exact cutoff used to separate NPH from other communicating hydrocephalus differs between guidelines.
The Laplace explanation of ventricular enlargement in NPH and the venous feedback loop in IIH are leading hypotheses, not established mechanisms.
The timing of peak edema after large infarcts (about 3 to 5 days) and the age of anterior fontanelle closure (about 12 to 18 months, sometimes up to 24) are approximate.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Kernohan notch, Duret hemorrhage, Dandy-Walker, and Chiari, and the term pseudotumor cerebri.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: csf-circulation (choroid plexus to arachnoid granulations, with obstruction sites marked) and herniation-syndromes (coronal brain showing subfalcine, uncal, central, and tonsillar herniation).
